title: the obligation nobody explains as a gift
hook: the obligation nobody explains as a gift
carry: one day that isn't yours to fill

segments.voice: Yesterday, confession, the most misunderstood room in the building. Your line was: say it out loud, then it's smaller. Did anything get smaller? Day thirteen.

Ask people who grew up Catholic what Sunday felt like, and you'll hear a lot of the same things. Being woken up too early. Scratchy church clothes. A parent saying, we're going, it's an obligation. The Sunday obligation: Catholics are asked to go to Mass every Sunday, and for a lot of kids it felt like homework for the soul. Now think about your own week. The phone that never stops. The laundry. The emails you answer on Saturday night. The feeling that every hour should be doing something. What if the obligation was never meant as homework? Today, Sunday, explained as a gift.
screen: `SCRATCHY CHURCH CLOTHES.` → `HOMEWORK FOR THE SOUL?` → `SUNDAY, EXPLAINED AS A GIFT.`

segments.voice: Start at the very beginning of the Bible. In Genesis, God makes the world in six days, and then, in the Douay-Rheims Bible, "he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done." God rests. Not because he's tired. The day of rest is built into the world like a beam into a house. For the Jewish people it became the Sabbath, the seventh day, kept from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday, and Jews still keep it. Then something happened on a different day. All four Gospels say the women found the tomb empty on the first day of the week, the day after the Sabbath. Christians began gathering on that day, the day of the resurrection. The last book of the Bible calls it by a new name: "I was in the spirit on the Lord's day." In Latin, dies Domini, the Lord's day. In Spanish it's still domingo, in Italian domenica. Around the year 150, a Christian named Justin Martyr described it for outsiders: on the day called Sunday, everyone gathers, the writings of the apostles are read, bread and wine are brought and blessed, and there's a collection for widows and orphans. That's recognizably the Mass from days three to five, nearly nineteen centuries ago. So why call it an obligation? Catholics say it's the way the Church makes sure the gift actually gets opened. Left to ourselves, most of us would fill every hour. The obligation holds one day open: for worship, for family, for rest, for a long meal. Sunday Mass can also be kept on Saturday evening, at what's called the vigil. The idea underneath is simple. One day a week isn't yours to fill.
screen: `HE RESTED ON THE SEVENTH DAY.` · `THE FIRST DAY: THE EMPTY TOMB.` · `DIES DOMINI — THE LORD'S DAY.` · `JUSTIN, AROUND 150: SUNDAY.` · then, large: `THE GIFT GETS OPENED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. A forty-five-second sit, and for these forty-five seconds, you have nothing to do. Nothing to fill. Put the phone face down, or out of reach. Let your hands rest open. Every time your mind reaches for a task, notice it, and set it down for later. If you pray, you can offer the time to God. If not, just let it be empty. The bell holds the time.
Sunday. The Lord's day, the day of the empty tomb, the day the Church keeps open for worship and rest. Thirteenth word.
Your line: one day that isn't yours to fill. Look at this week and pick a stretch of time, even an hour, that you'll leave empty on purpose. Day thirteen.
